people|Japanese people]] | litcolor = | longtype = Religious, cultural | significance = Day before the beginning of spring | scheduling = Varies | frequency = Annual | duration = 1 day | date = Between 2 and 4 February | celebrations = | observances = | relatedto = Spring Festival ({{transliteration|ja|Harumatsuri}}) | date2023 = Friday, 3 February | date2024 = Saturday, 3 February }} [[File:Setsubun 2006 Kobe.jpg|thumb|right|Celebrities throw roasted beans in [[Ikuta Shrine]], Kobe]] [[File:Kinpusenji Setsubune 2018a.jpg|thumb|[[:en:Kimpusen-ji|Kimpusen-ji]]]]
{{nihongo|||'''Setsubun'''}} is the day before the beginning of [[:en:Spring (season)|spring]] in the [[Japanese calendar|old calendar]] in [[:en:Japan|Japan]].<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p7sjIR5_LIAC&q=%22bean+throwing+festival&pg=PA61|page=61|title=The Naked Man Festival: And Other Excuses to Fly Around the World |first=Brian |last=Thacker |publisher=Allen & Unwin|year=2005 |isbn=1-74114-399-3}}</ref><ref name="sosnoski"/> The name literally means 'seasonal division', referring to the day just before the first day of spring in the traditional calendar, known as {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}; though previously referring to a wider range of possible dates, {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} is now typically held on February 3 (in 2021 it was on 2nd February),<ref name="geisha">{{cite book | title=Geisha | first=Liza Crihfield | last=Dalby | publisher=University of California Press | year=1983 | isbn=0-520-04742-7}}</ref> with the day after – the first day of spring in the old calendar – known as {{nihongo|||[[:en:Lichun|Risshun]]}}. Both {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} and {{transliteration|ja|Risshun}} are celebrated yearly as part of the Spring Festival ({{nihongo|||Haru matsuri}}) in Japan.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/religion/religions/shinto/holydays/harumatsuri.shtml |title=Religions – Shinto: Spring Matsuri (Spring festivals) |publisher=BBC |access-date=March 10, 2014}}</ref> {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} was accompanied by a number of [[:en:Ritual|Ritual]]s and traditions held at various levels to drive away the previous year's bad fortunes and [[:en:Obake|evil spirits]] for the year to come.<ref name="mie"/><ref name="dwc150119"/>
==History== {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} has its origins in {{nihongo|||[[:en:Nuo rituals|tsuina]]}}, a Chinese custom introduced to Japan in the 8th century.<ref name="sosnoski">{{cite book |title=Introduction to Japanese culture |first=Daniel |last=Sosnoski |publisher=Tuttle Publishing |year=1996 |isbn=0-8048-2056-2 |page=[https://archive.org/details/introductiontoja00dani/page/9 9] |url=https://archive.org/details/introductiontoja00dani |url-access=registration |quote=setsubun.}}</ref> It was quite different from the {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} known today. According to the Japanese history book {{transliteration|ja|[[Shoku Nihongi]]}}, {{transliteration|ja|tsuina}} was first held in Japan in 706, and it was an event to ward off evil spirits held at the court on the last day of the year according to the [[:en:en:Lunisolar calendar|lunar-solar calendar]]. At that time, {{transliteration|ja|tsuina}} was an event to drive away evil spirits that brought misfortune and disease by decorating each gate of the palace with clay figures of cows and children and using peach branches and walking sticks.<ref name="dazaifu">{{cite web|url=https://dazaifu-bunka.or.jp/info/letter/detail/57.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220815134519/https://dazaifu-bunka.or.jp/info/letter/detail/57.html|script-title=ja:伝えて行きたい伝統行事－節分－|language=ja|publisher=Dazaifu Fureai Museum|archive-date=15 August 2022|access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref><ref name="kikou">{{cite web|url=https://www.kikou.click/blog/entry-143834/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230204151314/https://www.kikou.click/blog/entry-143834/|script-title=ja:どうして豆まきをするの？ 節分の由来ご紹介|language=ja|publisher=Kikou|date=1 February 2019|archive-date=4 February 2023|access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sagae-hachimangu.org/news/news-273/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220927011942/https://www.sagae-hachimangu.org/news/news-273/|script-title=ja:節分|language=ja|publisher=[[:ja:寒河江八幡宮|Sagae Hachimangu]]|date=3 February 2022|archive-date=27 September 2022|access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref>
The custom of {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} as we know it today began in the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] (1336–1573). Every household of the aristocracy and [[:en:Samurai|Samurai]] class threw beans from their houses into the open air. The {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Ainōshō|ja|壒嚢鈔|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ainōshō|1=Ainōshō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11256759}}}},<ref>{{cite book|url=http://base1.nijl.ac.jp/iview/Frame.jsp?DB_ID=G0003917KTM&C_CODE=MA3-0097&IMG_SIZE=1000%2C800&PROC_TYPE=ON&SHOMEI=%E5%A3%92%E5%9B%8A%E9%88%94&REQUEST_MARK=%E3%83%9E%EF%BC%93%EF%BC%8D%EF%BC%99%EF%BC%97%EF%BC%8D%EF%BC%91%EF%BD%9E%EF%BC%91%EF%BC%95&OWNER=%E5%9B%BD%E6%96%87%E7%A0%94&IMG_NO=70|title=Ainōshō (壒嚢鈔)|author=Gyōyo (行誉)|publisher=[[National Institute of Japanese Literature]]|year=1445}}</ref> a dictionary compiled during the Muromachi period, states that the practice of bean-throwing during {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} originated from a legend in the 10th century, during the reign of [[:en:Emperor Uda|Emperor Uda]], that a monk on [[:en:Mount Kurama|Mt. Kurama]] escaped misfortune by blinding {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Oni|Oni]]}} with roasted beans. The Japanese word for bean, {{lang|ja|豆}}, is pronounced {{transliteration|ja|mame}}, which can be written as {{nihongo||魔目|{{gloss|devil's eye}}}}, and some believe that the pronunciation is similar to that of {{nihongo||魔滅|mametsu}}, meaning 'to destroy the devil', which is why people began throwing beans during {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}.<ref name="mie">{{cite web|url=https://www.bunka.pref.mie.lg.jp/rekishi/kenshi/asp/hakken/detail.asp?record=303|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211201054231/https://www.bunka.pref.mie.lg.jp/rekishi/kenshi/asp/hakken/detail.asp?record=303|script-title=ja:節分行事あれこれ 薄れる「年頭」感覚－風習、呼び名 地域で特色|language=ja|publisher=[[:en:Mie Prefecture|Mie Prefecture]]|date=|archive-date=1 December 2021|access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nippon.com/ja/guide-to-japan/gu900080/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220624133557/https://www.nippon.com/ja/guide-to-japan/gu900080/|script-title=ja:勇壮で華やかな京都の節分：吉田神社の追儺式、蘆山寺の鬼おどり、八坂神社の豆まき|language=ja|publisher=nippon.com|date=31 January 2019|archive-date=24 June 2022|access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref><ref name="kikou"/>
From the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] (1603–1867), the custom of throwing beans at [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]], [[:en:Buddhist temples in Japan|Buddhist temples]], and homes of ordinary people spread throughout Japan as an event or festival to drive away evil spirits during {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}. It was also during this period that the custom of tying roasted sardine heads to [[:en:Holly|Holly]] sprig to decorate the gates of houses during {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} began. This custom was intended to scare away {{transliteration|ja|oni}} with the thorns of the holly leaves and the smell of the roasted sardines. The original form of this custom is recorded in the {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Tosa Nikki|Tosa Nikki]]}}, compiled in 934 during the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] (794–1185). The diary describes a [[Shinto]] {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Shimenawa|Shimenawa]]}} (sacred rope) that was hung on the gate of a house during the New Year's holiday to mark the boundary of purification, and that a [[:en:Mullet (fish)|mullet]] head pierced with a sprig of holly was attached to the {{transliteration|ja|shimenawa}}.<ref name="mie"/><ref name="dwc150119">{{cite web|url=https://www.dwc.doshisha.ac.jp/research/faculty_column/2019-01-15-12-55|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210201235325/https://www.dwc.doshisha.ac.jp/research/faculty_column/2019-01-15-12-55|script-title=ja:節分の「鰯の頭」と「柊鰯」|language=ja|publisher=[[Doshisha Women's College of Liberal Arts]]|date=15 January 2019|archive-date=1 February 2021|access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref>
The custom of eating {{nihongo||恵方巻|ehōmaki}} on {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} began in the [[:en:Geisha|Geisha]] districts from the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] to the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]]. {{transliteration|ja|Ehōmaki}} is a special {{transliteration|ja|[[Sushi#Makizushi|makizushi]]}} ([[:en:Sushi|Sushi]] roll) eaten on {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}. On {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}, people face the most auspicious direction of the year and eat the whole {{transliteration|ja|ehōmaki}}, an uncut sushi roll, to pray for prosperity and happiness for the year. It is believed that it was originally called simply {{nihongo||丸かぶり寿司|marukaburi zushi}} or {{nihongo||太巻き寿司|futomaki zushi}}. The name {{transliteration|ja|ehōmaki}} may have spread throughout Japan in 1989, when a Japanese convenience store chain renamed it {{transliteration|ja|ehōmaki}} and began selling it.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://r.gnavi.co.jp/food/sushi/ehoumaki/ehoumaki_04.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230202124725/https://r.gnavi.co.jp/food/sushi/ehoumaki/ehoumaki_04.html|script-title=ja:仕掛けた人は誰？恵方巻きの由来・ルーツ・丸かぶりの謎|language=ja|publisher=Gurunavi|archive-date=2 February 2023|access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref>
==Traditions== ==={{transliteration|ja|Mamemaki}}=== The main ritual associated with the observance of {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} is {{nihongo3|{{gloss|bean scattering}}||mamemaki}}; this ritual sees roasted [[:en:Soybean|Soybean]]s (known as {{nihongo3|{{gloss|fortune beans}}|福豆|fukumame}}) either thrown out of the front door, or at a member of the family wearing an {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Oni|Oni]]}} ([[:en:Demon|Demon]] or [[:en:Ogre|Ogre]]) mask while shouting {{nihongo|{{gloss|Devils out! Fortune in!}}|鬼は外! 福は内!|Oni wa soto! Fuku wa uchi!}},<ref name="geisha"/> before slamming the door.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Vvw5WQ0crLoC&q=Setsubun&pg=PA194|page=194|title=Japan pop!: inside the world of Japanese popular culture| first=Timothy J. |last=Craig |publisher=M.E. Sharpe|year=2000 |isbn=0-7656-0561-9}}</ref> The beans are thought to symbolically [[Ritual purification|purify]] the home by driving away the evil spirits that bring misfortune and bad health with them. Then, as part of bringing [[:en:en:Luck|en:Luck]] in, it is customary to eat roasted [[:en:Soybean|Soybean]]s, one for each year of one's life ({{transliteration|ja|[[:en:East Asian age reckoning|kazoedoshi]]}}), plus one more for bringing good luck for the year.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2FXOagNuv0wC&q=Setsubun&pg=PA62|page=62|title=An Illustrated History of the Haunted World |first=Jason |last=Karl |publisher=New Holland Publishers|year=2007 |isbn=978-1-84537-687-1}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dltk-kids.com/World/japan/index-setsubun.htm|title = Japanese Setsubun Festival Activities}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://workinjapan.today/culture/all-about-setsubun-the-bean-throwing-festival/|title = All About Setsubun: The Bean-Throwing Festival | Work in Japan for engineers|date = January 19, 2021}}</ref>
The custom of {{transliteration|ja|mamemaki}} first appeared in the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]],<ref name="sosnoski"/> and is usually performed by either a man of the household born in the corresponding [[:en:Chinese zodiac|zodiac]] year for the new year ({{nihongo||年男|toshiotoko}}), or else the male head of the household.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://skywardplus.jal.co.jp/plus_one/calendar/setsubun/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230202134059/https://skywardplus.jal.co.jp/plus_one/calendar/setsubun/|script-title=ja:節分とは？2023rd year は2月3日 豆まきや恵方巻の意味と由来|language=ja|publisher=[[Japan Airlines]]|date=18 January 2023|archive-date=2 February 2023|access-date=5 February 2023}}</ref>
Because [[:en:Watanabe no Tsuna|Watanabe no Tsuna]], a retainer of [[:en:Minamoto no Yorimitsu|Minamoto no Yorimitsu]] during the Heian period (794–1185), is associated with the legend that he vanquished {{transliteration|ja|oni}} historically considered to be the strongest, such as [[:en:Shuten-doji|Shuten-doji]] and [[:en:Ibaraki-doji|Ibaraki-doji]], there is a tradition that {{transliteration|ja|oni}} stay away from people named [[:en:Watanabe|Watanabe]] and their houses. For this reason, some families with the surname Watanabe have not practiced the custom of throwing beans on Setsubun for generations.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.kobe-np.co.jp/news/hanshin/202202/0015034626.shtml|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230202170621/https://www.kobe-np.co.jp/news/hanshin/202202/0015034626.shtml|script-title=ja:渡辺さんは豆まきしない？ 最後に「鬼は内～」 阪神間の多彩な「鬼事情」|language=ja|publisher=[[Kobe Shimbun]]|date=3 February 2022|archive-date=2 February 2023|access-date=5 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.livedoor.com/article/detail/12625711/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210202012629/https://news.livedoor.com/article/detail/12625711/|script-title=ja:「渡辺姓」の人は豆まきをしなくていい理由 平安時代の歴史に起因|language=ja|publisher=Livedoor News|date=3 February 2017|archive-date=2 February 2021|access-date=5 February 2023}}</ref> Watanabe no Tsuna was the first person to take the surname Watanabe, and Watanabe is the fifth most common surname in Japan, with approximately 1.08 million people {{as of|2017|lc=y}}.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://toyokeizai.net/articles/-/173199|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230130002443/https://toyokeizai.net/articles/-/173199|script-title=ja:｢渡辺｣｢渡部｣｢渡邊｣｢渡邉｣の知られざる真実|page=1,2|language=ja|publisher=[[Toyo Keizai]]|date=28 May 2017|archive-date=30 January 2023|access-date=5 February 2023}}</ref>
Though still a somewhat common practice in households, many people will also or instead attend a shrine or temple's spring festival, where the practice of {{transliteration|ja|mamemaki}} is performed;<ref name="geisha"/> in some areas, such as [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]], this involves a dance performed by [[:en:Maiko|apprentice geisha]], after which the apprentices themselves throw packets of roasted soybeans to the crowds. In other areas, priests and invited guests throw packets of roasted soybeans, some wrapped in gold or silver foil, small envelopes with money, sweets, candies and other prizes. In some bigger and more central shrines, celebrities and [[:en:Sumo|Sumo]] wrestlers are invited to celebrations, usually to {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} events that are televised.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://gojapan.about.com/cs/japanesefestivals/a/setsubun.htm | title=Setsubun – Bean Throwing Festival | first=Shizuko | last=Mishima | publisher=[[About.com]] | access-date=February 1, 2011 | archive-date=July 7, 2011 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110707075210/http://gojapan.about.com/cs/japanesefestivals/a/setsubun.htm | url-status=dead }}</ref> At [[Sensō-ji]] in the [[:en:Asakusa, Tokyo|Asakusa]] neighborhood of Tokyo, crowds of nearly 100,000 people attend the annual festivities.<ref name="JTB">{{cite web | url=http://blog.jtbusa.com/all/setsubun-is-right-around-the-corner | publisher=[[Japan Travel Bureau]] | title=Setsubun Is Right Around the Corner | date=January 29, 2014 | access-date=February 2, 2014 | archive-date=February 19, 2014 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140219030657/http://blog.jtbusa.com/all/setsubun-is-right-around-the-corner | url-status=dead }}</ref>
===Other practices=== [[File:Setsubun, hiragi iwashi.JPG|thumb|Sardine head talisman on house entrance to keep bad spirits away]]
A number of other, in some cases more esoteric practices exist surrounding the celebration and observance of {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}; some are regional, such as the [[:en:Kansai region|Kansai region]] area tradition of eating uncut {{transliteration|ja|[[sushi#makizushi|makizushi]]}} rolls, known as {{nihongo3|{{gloss|lucky direction roll}}|恵方巻|ehō-maki}}, in silence whilst facing the year's lucky compass direction as determined by the zodiac symbol of that year.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://web.mit.edu/jpnet/holidays/Feb/setsubun.shtml | title=Setsubun – Around February 3 | publisher=[[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] | date=March 5, 2002 | access-date=February 2, 2014}}</ref> Though the custom originated in [[:en:Osaka|Osaka]], it has since spread, due largely to marketing efforts by grocery and convenience stores.<ref>{{cite news | url=http://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2002/02/03/food/are-you-ready-to-roll-with-the-change-on-setsubun-no-hi/#.Uu33w7TaeHI | title=Are you ready to roll with the change on 'setsubun no hi'? | work=[[:en:The Japan Times|The Japan Times]] | first=Rick | last=Lapointe | date=February 3, 2002 | access-date=February 2, 2014}}</ref>
Other practices include the putting up of small decorations of [[:en:sardine|sardine]] heads and {{nihongo|holly leaves|柊鰯|hiiragi iwashi}} at the entrance to a house to ward off evil spirits.<ref name="geisha"/> A special variety of [[sake]] known as {{nihongo||生姜酒|shōgazake}} brewed with ginger is also customarily drunk on {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}. Each region of Japan has its own lucky charms to eat on {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}. Soybeans used for {{transliteration|ja|mamemaki}} and [[:en:Soba|Soba]] are the most common, but [[:en:peanut|peanut]]s in the [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaidō]] and [[:en:Tōhoku region|Tōhoku region]], {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Kenchin-jiru|Kenchin-jiru]]}} and {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:shimotsukare|shimotsukare]]}} in the [[:en:Kanto region|Kanto region]], tea with [[:en:kelp|kelp]] and sardines in [[:en:Kansai region|Kansai region]], [[:en:Konjac|Konjac]] in [[:en:Shikoku region|Shikoku region]], [[:en:Sea cucumber|Sea cucumber]] in the [[:en:Oki Islands|Oki Islands]], and [[:en:Whale|Whale]] in the [[:en:San'in region|San'in region]] are also eaten.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://allabout.co.jp/gm/gc/220642/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240222115643/https://allabout.co.jp/gm/gc/220642/|script-title=ja:鬼は内？鬼は外？豆まき珍風習や、恵方巻以外もある各地の節分行事食|page=|language=ja|publisher=All About,inc|date=27 December 2023|archive-date=22 February 2024|access-date=8 March 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://web.hh-online.jp/hankyu-food/blog/lifestyle/detail/001183.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240308120038/https://web.hh-online.jp/hankyu-food/blog/lifestyle/detail/001183.html|script-title=ja:節分の食べ物は地域によって違う？意味や由来も紹介|page=|language=ja|publisher=Hankyu Hanshin Department Stores, Inc.|date=23 September 2022|archive-date=8 March 2024|access-date=8 March 2024}}</ref>
==Historical practices== The new year was felt to be a time when the spirit world became close to the physical world, thus the need to perform {{transliteration|ja|mamemaki}} to drive away any [[:en:wandering spirits|wandering spirits]] that might happen too close to one's home. Other customs during this time included [[:en:ceremonial dance|religious dances]], [[:en:Festivals|Festivals]], and bringing tools inside the house that might normally be left outside, to prevent the spirits from harming them. Rice cakes were also balanced on lintels and windowsills.<ref name="geisha"/>
Because {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} is considered to be a day set apart from the rest of the year, a tradition of role reversal in appearance and dress was also practiced; such customs included girls wearing the [[:en:nihongami#brides|hairstyles]] of older women and vice versa, wearing disguises, and [[:en:Cross-dressing|Cross-dressing]]. This custom is still practiced among [[:en:Geisha|Geisha]] and their clients when entertaining on {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}.<ref name="geisha"/>
{{nihongo|Traveling entertainers|旅芸人|tabi geinin}}, who were normally shunned during the year because they were considered [[:en:Vagrancy (people)|vagrant]]s, were welcomed on {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} to perform [[:en:Ethics|morality]] plays. Their vagrancy worked to their advantage in these cases, as they were considered to take evil spirits with them.<ref name="geisha"/>{{rp|121}}
==Regional variations== In the [[:en:Tōhoku|Tōhoku]] area of Japan, the head of the household (traditionally the father) would take roasted beans in his hand, pray at the [[Kamidana|family shrine]], and then toss the sanctified beans out the door.<ref name="ShurtleffAoyagi2012">{{cite book|last1=Shurtleff|first1=William|last2=Aoyagi|first2=Akiko|title=History of Soynuts, Soynut Butter, Japanese-Style Roasted Soybeans (Irimame) and Setsubun (with Mamemaki) (1068–2012): Extensively Annotated Bibliography and Sourcebook|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KEC_dDHw_88C&pg=PA521|access-date=February 2, 2018|date=December 2012|publisher=Soyinfo Center|isbn=9781928914532|page=521}}</ref> Peanuts (either raw or coated in a sweet, crunchy batter) are sometimes used in place of soybeans.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.jref.com/japan/culture/setsubun.shtml | title=Setsubun 節分 | date=February 2, 2013 | publisher=Japan Reference | access-date=February 2, 2014}}</ref>
There are many variations on the famous {{transliteration|ja|"Oni wa soto, fuku wa uchi!"}} chant. For example, in the city of [[:en:Aizuwakamatsu|Aizuwakamatsu]], people chant {{nihongo3|{{gloss|Blind the demons' eyes!}}|鬼の目玉ぶっつぶせ！|Oni no medama buttsubuse!}}<ref name="ShurtleffAoyagi2012"/>
==See also== {{Portal|Japan}} * {{transliteration|ja|[[Sushi#Ehomaki|Ehōmaki]]}}, a sushi roll often eaten for good luck on {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}. * [[:en:Exorcism|Exorcism]] * [[:en:Feast of the Lemures|Feast of the Lemures]] (a similar Roman custom) * [[:en:Holidays of Japan|Holidays of Japan]] * {{nihongo||立夏|1=Lixia|[[:en:Lixia|Rikka]]}} * {{nihongo||立秋|[[:en:Liqiu|Risshū]]}} * {{nihongo||立春|1=Lichun|lt=Risshun|[[:en:Lichun|Risshun]]}} * {{nihongo||立冬|[[:en:Lidong|Rittō]]}} * [[:en:Saint John's Eve|Saint John's Eve]] * [[:en:Taoism in Japan|Taoism in Japan]] * [[:en:Walpurgis Night|Walpurgis Night]] * [[:en:Zvončari|Zvončari]] (the custom dating to pagan times in [[:en:Croatia|Croatia]] whose goal is to scare away evil spirits of winter and to stir up new springtime cycle)

{{nihongo|||'''Setsubun'''}} is the day before the beginning of {{ill|Spring (season)|en|Spring (season)|WD=Q1312|lt=spring}} in the [[Japanese calendar|old calendar]] in {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan}}.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p7sjIR5_LIAC&q=%22bean+throwing+festival&pg=PA61|page=61|title=The Naked Man Festival: And Other Excuses to Fly Around the World |first=Brian |last=Thacker |publisher=Allen & Unwin|year=2005 |isbn=1-74114-399-3}}</ref><ref name="sosnoski"/> The name literally means 'seasonal division', referring to the day just before the first day of spring in the traditional calendar, known as {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}; though previously referring to a wider range of possible dates, {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} is now typically held on February 3 (in 2021 it was on 2nd February),<ref name="geisha">{{cite book | title=Geisha | first=Liza Crihfield | last=Dalby | publisher=University of California Press | year=1983 | isbn=0-520-04742-7}}</ref> with the day after – the first day of spring in the old calendar – known as {{nihongo|||{{ill|Lichun|en|Lichun|WD=Q1364685|lt=Risshun}}}}. Both {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} and {{transliteration|ja|Risshun}} are celebrated yearly as part of the Spring Festival ({{nihongo|||Haru matsuri}}) in Japan.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/religion/religions/shinto/holydays/harumatsuri.shtml |title=Religions – Shinto: Spring Matsuri (Spring festivals) |publisher=BBC |access-date=March 10, 2014}}</ref> {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} was accompanied by a number of {{ill|Ritual|en|Ritual|WD=Q189819|lt=Ritual}}s and traditions held at various levels to drive away the previous year's bad fortunes and {{ill|Obake|en|Obake|WD=Q1639284|lt=evil spirits}} for the year to come.<ref name="mie"/><ref name="dwc150119"/>
==History== {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} has its origins in {{nihongo|||[[:en:Nuo rituals|tsuina]]}}, a Chinese custom introduced to Japan in the 8th century.<ref name="sosnoski">{{cite book |title=Introduction to Japanese culture |first=Daniel |last=Sosnoski |publisher=Tuttle Publishing |year=1996 |isbn=0-8048-2056-2 |page=[https://archive.org/details/introductiontoja00dani/page/9 9] |url=https://archive.org/details/introductiontoja00dani |url-access=registration |quote=setsubun.}}</ref> It was quite different from the {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} known today. According to the Japanese history book {{transliteration|ja|[[Shoku Nihongi]]}}, {{transliteration|ja|tsuina}} was first held in Japan in 706, and it was an event to ward off evil spirits held at the court on the last day of the year according to the {{ill|en:Lunisolar calendar|en|en:Lunisolar calendar|WD=Q194235|lt=lunar-solar calendar}}. At that time, {{transliteration|ja|tsuina}} was an event to drive away evil spirits that brought misfortune and disease by decorating each gate of the palace with clay figures of cows and children and using peach branches and walking sticks.<ref name="dazaifu">{{cite web|url=https://dazaifu-bunka.or.jp/info/letter/detail/57.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220815134519/https://dazaifu-bunka.or.jp/info/letter/detail/57.html|script-title=ja:伝えて行きたい伝統行事－節分－|language=ja|publisher=Dazaifu Fureai Museum|archive-date=15 August 2022|access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref><ref name="kikou">{{cite web|url=https://www.kikou.click/blog/entry-143834/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230204151314/https://www.kikou.click/blog/entry-143834/|script-title=ja:どうして豆まきをするの？ 節分の由来ご紹介|language=ja|publisher=Kikou|date=1 February 2019|archive-date=4 February 2023|access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sagae-hachimangu.org/news/news-273/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220927011942/https://www.sagae-hachimangu.org/news/news-273/|script-title=ja:節分|language=ja|publisher=[[:ja:寒河江八幡宮|Sagae Hachimangu]]|date=3 February 2022|archive-date=27 September 2022|access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref>
The custom of {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} as we know it today began in the {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}} (1336–1573). Every household of the aristocracy and {{ill|Samurai|en|Samurai|WD=Q38142|lt=Samurai}} class threw beans from their houses into the open air. The {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Ainōshō|ja|壒嚢鈔|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ainōshō|1=Ainōshō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11256759}}}},<ref>{{cite book|url=http://base1.nijl.ac.jp/iview/Frame.jsp?DB_ID=G0003917KTM&C_CODE=MA3-0097&IMG_SIZE=1000%2C800&PROC_TYPE=ON&SHOMEI=%E5%A3%92%E5%9B%8A%E9%88%94&REQUEST_MARK=%E3%83%9E%EF%BC%93%EF%BC%8D%EF%BC%99%EF%BC%97%EF%BC%8D%EF%BC%91%EF%BD%9E%EF%BC%91%EF%BC%95&OWNER=%E5%9B%BD%E6%96%87%E7%A0%94&IMG_NO=70|title=Ainōshō (壒嚢鈔)|author=Gyōyo (行誉)|publisher=[[National Institute of Japanese Literature]]|year=1445}}</ref> a dictionary compiled during the Muromachi period, states that the practice of bean-throwing during {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} originated from a legend in the 10th century, during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Uda|en|Emperor Uda|WD=Q349267|lt=Emperor Uda}}, that a monk on {{ill|Mount Kurama|en|Mount Kurama|WD=Q410132|lt=Mt. Kurama}} escaped misfortune by blinding {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Oni|en|Oni|WD=Q730052|lt=Oni}}}} with roasted beans. The Japanese word for bean, {{lang|ja|豆}}, is pronounced {{transliteration|ja|mame}}, which can be written as {{nihongo||魔目|{{gloss|devil's eye}}}}, and some believe that the pronunciation is similar to that of {{nihongo||魔滅|mametsu}}, meaning 'to destroy the devil', which is why people began throwing beans during {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}.<ref name="mie">{{cite web|url=https://www.bunka.pref.mie.lg.jp/rekishi/kenshi/asp/hakken/detail.asp?record=303|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211201054231/https://www.bunka.pref.mie.lg.jp/rekishi/kenshi/asp/hakken/detail.asp?record=303|script-title=ja:節分行事あれこれ 薄れる「年頭」感覚－風習、呼び名 地域で特色|language=ja|publisher={{ill|Mie Prefecture|en|Mie Prefecture|WD=Q128196|lt=Mie Prefecture}}|date=|archive-date=1 December 2021|access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nippon.com/ja/guide-to-japan/gu900080/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220624133557/https://www.nippon.com/ja/guide-to-japan/gu900080/|script-title=ja:勇壮で華やかな京都の節分：吉田神社の追儺式、蘆山寺の鬼おどり、八坂神社の豆まき|language=ja|publisher=nippon.com|date=31 January 2019|archive-date=24 June 2022|access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref><ref name="kikou"/>
From the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} (1603–1867), the custom of throwing beans at {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}}, {{ill|Buddhist temples in Japan|en|Buddhist temples in Japan|WD=Q3141900|lt=Buddhist temples}}, and homes of ordinary people spread throughout Japan as an event or festival to drive away evil spirits during {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}. It was also during this period that the custom of tying roasted sardine heads to {{ill|Holly|en|Holly|WD=Q117085|lt=Holly}} sprig to decorate the gates of houses during {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} began. This custom was intended to scare away {{transliteration|ja|oni}} with the thorns of the holly leaves and the smell of the roasted sardines. The original form of this custom is recorded in the {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Tosa Nikki|en|Tosa Nikki|WD=Q844452|lt=Tosa Nikki}}}}, compiled in 934 during the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}} (794–1185). The diary describes a [[Shinto]] {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa}}}} (sacred rope) that was hung on the gate of a house during the New Year's holiday to mark the boundary of purification, and that a {{ill|Mullet (fish)|en|Mullet (fish)|WD=Q42237|lt=mullet}} head pierced with a sprig of holly was attached to the {{transliteration|ja|shimenawa}}.<ref name="mie"/><ref name="dwc150119">{{cite web|url=https://www.dwc.doshisha.ac.jp/research/faculty_column/2019-01-15-12-55|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210201235325/https://www.dwc.doshisha.ac.jp/research/faculty_column/2019-01-15-12-55|script-title=ja:節分の「鰯の頭」と「柊鰯」|language=ja|publisher=[[Doshisha Women's College of Liberal Arts]]|date=15 January 2019|archive-date=1 February 2021|access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref>
The custom of eating {{nihongo||恵方巻|ehōmaki}} on {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} began in the {{ill|Geisha|en|Geisha|WD=Q82723|lt=Geisha}} districts from the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} to the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era}}. {{transliteration|ja|Ehōmaki}} is a special {{transliteration|ja|[[Sushi#Makizushi|makizushi]]}} ({{ill|Sushi|en|Sushi|WD=Q46383|lt=Sushi}} roll) eaten on {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}. On {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}, people face the most auspicious direction of the year and eat the whole {{transliteration|ja|ehōmaki}}, an uncut sushi roll, to pray for prosperity and happiness for the year. It is believed that it was originally called simply {{nihongo||丸かぶり寿司|marukaburi zushi}} or {{nihongo||太巻き寿司|futomaki zushi}}. The name {{transliteration|ja|ehōmaki}} may have spread throughout Japan in 1989, when a Japanese convenience store chain renamed it {{transliteration|ja|ehōmaki}} and began selling it.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://r.gnavi.co.jp/food/sushi/ehoumaki/ehoumaki_04.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230202124725/https://r.gnavi.co.jp/food/sushi/ehoumaki/ehoumaki_04.html|script-title=ja:仕掛けた人は誰？恵方巻きの由来・ルーツ・丸かぶりの謎|language=ja|publisher=Gurunavi|archive-date=2 February 2023|access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref>
==Traditions== ==={{transliteration|ja|Mamemaki}}=== The main ritual associated with the observance of {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} is {{nihongo3|{{gloss|bean scattering}}||mamemaki}}; this ritual sees roasted {{ill|Soybean|en|Soybean|WD=Q11006|lt=Soybean}}s (known as {{nihongo3|{{gloss|fortune beans}}|福豆|fukumame}}) either thrown out of the front door, or at a member of the family wearing an {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Oni|en|Oni|WD=Q730052|lt=Oni}}}} ({{ill|Demon|en|Demon|WD=Q177413|lt=Demon}} or {{ill|Ogre|en|Ogre|WD=Q290562|lt=Ogre}}) mask while shouting {{nihongo|{{gloss|Devils out! Fortune in!}}|鬼は外! 福は内!|Oni wa soto! Fuku wa uchi!}},<ref name="geisha"/> before slamming the door.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Vvw5WQ0crLoC&q=Setsubun&pg=PA194|page=194|title=Japan pop!: inside the world of Japanese popular culture| first=Timothy J. |last=Craig |publisher=M.E. Sharpe|year=2000 |isbn=0-7656-0561-9}}</ref> The beans are thought to symbolically [[Ritual purification|purify]] the home by driving away the evil spirits that bring misfortune and bad health with them. Then, as part of bringing {{ill|en:Luck|en|en:Luck|WD=Q1970348|lt=en:Luck}} in, it is customary to eat roasted {{ill|Soybean|en|Soybean|WD=Q11006|lt=Soybean}}s, one for each year of one's life ({{transliteration|ja|{{ill|East Asian age reckoning|en|East Asian age reckoning|WD=Q850273|lt=kazoedoshi}}}}), plus one more for bringing good luck for the year.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2FXOagNuv0wC&q=Setsubun&pg=PA62|page=62|title=An Illustrated History of the Haunted World |first=Jason |last=Karl |publisher=New Holland Publishers|year=2007 |isbn=978-1-84537-687-1}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dltk-kids.com/World/japan/index-setsubun.htm|title = Japanese Setsubun Festival Activities}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://workinjapan.today/culture/all-about-setsubun-the-bean-throwing-festival/|title = All About Setsubun: The Bean-Throwing Festival | Work in Japan for engineers|date = January 19, 2021}}</ref>
The custom of {{transliteration|ja|mamemaki}} first appeared in the {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}},<ref name="sosnoski"/> and is usually performed by either a man of the household born in the corresponding {{ill|Chinese zodiac|en|Chinese zodiac|WD=Q1976204|lt=zodiac}} year for the new year ({{nihongo||年男|toshiotoko}}), or else the male head of the household.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://skywardplus.jal.co.jp/plus_one/calendar/setsubun/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230202134059/https://skywardplus.jal.co.jp/plus_one/calendar/setsubun/|script-title=ja:節分とは？2023rd year は2月3日 豆まきや恵方巻の意味と由来|language=ja|publisher=[[Japan Airlines]]|date=18 January 2023|archive-date=2 February 2023|access-date=5 February 2023}}</ref>
Because {{ill|Watanabe no Tsuna|en|Watanabe no Tsuna|WD=Q6582069|lt=Watanabe no Tsuna}}, a retainer of {{ill|Minamoto no Yorimitsu|en|Minamoto no Yorimitsu|WD=Q590523|lt=Minamoto no Yorimitsu}} during the Heian period (794–1185), is associated with the legend that he vanquished {{transliteration|ja|oni}} historically considered to be the strongest, such as [[:en:Shuten-doji|Shuten-doji]] and [[:en:Ibaraki-doji|Ibaraki-doji]], there is a tradition that {{transliteration|ja|oni}} stay away from people named {{ill|Watanabe|en|Watanabe|WD=Q10983405|lt=Watanabe}} and their houses. For this reason, some families with the surname Watanabe have not practiced the custom of throwing beans on Setsubun for generations.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.kobe-np.co.jp/news/hanshin/202202/0015034626.shtml|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230202170621/https://www.kobe-np.co.jp/news/hanshin/202202/0015034626.shtml|script-title=ja:渡辺さんは豆まきしない？ 最後に「鬼は内～」 阪神間の多彩な「鬼事情」|language=ja|publisher=[[Kobe Shimbun]]|date=3 February 2022|archive-date=2 February 2023|access-date=5 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.livedoor.com/article/detail/12625711/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210202012629/https://news.livedoor.com/article/detail/12625711/|script-title=ja:「渡辺姓」の人は豆まきをしなくていい理由 平安時代の歴史に起因|language=ja|publisher=Livedoor News|date=3 February 2017|archive-date=2 February 2021|access-date=5 February 2023}}</ref> Watanabe no Tsuna was the first person to take the surname Watanabe, and Watanabe is the fifth most common surname in Japan, with approximately 1.08 million people {{as of|2017|lc=y}}.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://toyokeizai.net/articles/-/173199|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230130002443/https://toyokeizai.net/articles/-/173199|script-title=ja:｢渡辺｣｢渡部｣｢渡邊｣｢渡邉｣の知られざる真実|page=1,2|language=ja|publisher=[[Toyo Keizai]]|date=28 May 2017|archive-date=30 January 2023|access-date=5 February 2023}}</ref>
Though still a somewhat common practice in households, many people will also or instead attend a shrine or temple's spring festival, where the practice of {{transliteration|ja|mamemaki}} is performed;<ref name="geisha"/> in some areas, such as {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}}, this involves a dance performed by {{ill|Maiko|en|Maiko|WD=Q616856|lt=apprentice geisha}}, after which the apprentices themselves throw packets of roasted soybeans to the crowds. In other areas, priests and invited guests throw packets of roasted soybeans, some wrapped in gold or silver foil, small envelopes with money, sweets, candies and other prizes. In some bigger and more central shrines, celebrities and {{ill|Sumo|en|Sumo|WD=Q40561|lt=Sumo}} wrestlers are invited to celebrations, usually to {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} events that are televised.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://gojapan.about.com/cs/japanesefestivals/a/setsubun.htm | title=Setsubun – Bean Throwing Festival | first=Shizuko | last=Mishima | publisher=[[About.com]] | access-date=February 1, 2011 | archive-date=July 7, 2011 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110707075210/http://gojapan.about.com/cs/japanesefestivals/a/setsubun.htm | url-status=dead }}</ref> At [[Sensō-ji]] in the [[:en:Asakusa, Tokyo|Asakusa]] neighborhood of Tokyo, crowds of nearly 100,000 people attend the annual festivities.<ref name="JTB">{{cite web | url=http://blog.jtbusa.com/all/setsubun-is-right-around-the-corner | publisher=[[Japan Travel Bureau]] | title=Setsubun Is Right Around the Corner | date=January 29, 2014 | access-date=February 2, 2014 | archive-date=February 19, 2014 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140219030657/http://blog.jtbusa.com/all/setsubun-is-right-around-the-corner | url-status=dead }}</ref>
===Other practices=== [[File:Setsubun, hiragi iwashi.JPG|thumb|Sardine head talisman on house entrance to keep bad spirits away]]
A number of other, in some cases more esoteric practices exist surrounding the celebration and observance of {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}; some are regional, such as the {{ill|Kansai region|en|Kansai region|WD=Q164256|lt=Kansai region}} area tradition of eating uncut {{transliteration|ja|[[sushi#makizushi|makizushi]]}} rolls, known as {{nihongo3|{{gloss|lucky direction roll}}|恵方巻|ehō-maki}}, in silence whilst facing the year's lucky compass direction as determined by the zodiac symbol of that year.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://web.mit.edu/jpnet/holidays/Feb/setsubun.shtml | title=Setsubun – Around February 3 | publisher=[[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] | date=March 5, 2002 | access-date=February 2, 2014}}</ref> Though the custom originated in {{ill|Osaka|en|Osaka|WD=Q35765|lt=Osaka}}, it has since spread, due largely to marketing efforts by grocery and convenience stores.<ref>{{cite news | url=http://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2002/02/03/food/are-you-ready-to-roll-with-the-change-on-setsubun-no-hi/#.Uu33w7TaeHI | title=Are you ready to roll with the change on 'setsubun no hi'? | work={{ill|The Japan Times|en|The Japan Times|WD=Q1190886|lt=The Japan Times}} | first=Rick | last=Lapointe | date=February 3, 2002 | access-date=February 2, 2014}}</ref>
Other practices include the putting up of small decorations of {{ill|sardine|en|sardine|WD=Q5141254|lt=sardine}} heads and {{nihongo|holly leaves|柊鰯|hiiragi iwashi}} at the entrance to a house to ward off evil spirits.<ref name="geisha"/> A special variety of [[sake]] known as {{nihongo||生姜酒|shōgazake}} brewed with ginger is also customarily drunk on {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}. Each region of Japan has its own lucky charms to eat on {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}. Soybeans used for {{transliteration|ja|mamemaki}} and {{ill|Soba|en|Soba|WD=Q753910|lt=Soba}} are the most common, but {{ill|peanut|en|peanut|WD=Q37383|lt=peanut}}s in the [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaidō]] and {{ill|Tōhoku region|en|Tōhoku region|WD=Q129465|lt=Tōhoku region}}, {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Kenchin-jiru|en|Kenchin-jiru|WD=Q11266028|lt=Kenchin-jiru}}}} and {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|shimotsukare|en|shimotsukare|WD=Q1002865|lt=shimotsukare}}}} in the [[:en:Kanto region|Kanto region]], tea with {{ill|kelp|en|kelp|WD=Q1055316|lt=kelp}} and sardines in {{ill|Kansai region|en|Kansai region|WD=Q164256|lt=Kansai region}}, [[:en:Konjac|Konjac]] in [[:en:Shikoku region|Shikoku region]], {{ill|Sea cucumber|en|Sea cucumber|WD=Q127470|lt=Sea cucumber}} in the {{ill|Oki Islands|en|Oki Islands|WD=Q483146|lt=Oki Islands}}, and {{ill|Whale|en|Whale|WD=Q1865281|lt=Whale}} in the {{ill|San'in region|en|San'in region|WD=Q398310|lt=San'in region}} are also eaten.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://allabout.co.jp/gm/gc/220642/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240222115643/https://allabout.co.jp/gm/gc/220642/|script-title=ja:鬼は内？鬼は外？豆まき珍風習や、恵方巻以外もある各地の節分行事食|page=|language=ja|publisher=All About,inc|date=27 December 2023|archive-date=22 February 2024|access-date=8 March 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://web.hh-online.jp/hankyu-food/blog/lifestyle/detail/001183.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240308120038/https://web.hh-online.jp/hankyu-food/blog/lifestyle/detail/001183.html|script-title=ja:節分の食べ物は地域によって違う？意味や由来も紹介|page=|language=ja|publisher=Hankyu Hanshin Department Stores, Inc.|date=23 September 2022|archive-date=8 March 2024|access-date=8 March 2024}}</ref>
==Historical practices== The new year was felt to be a time when the spirit world became close to the physical world, thus the need to perform {{transliteration|ja|mamemaki}} to drive away any [[:en:wandering spirits|wandering spirits]] that might happen too close to one's home. Other customs during this time included {{ill|ceremonial dance|en|ceremonial dance|WD=Q3595906|lt=religious dances}}, [[:en:Festivals|Festivals]], and bringing tools inside the house that might normally be left outside, to prevent the spirits from harming them. Rice cakes were also balanced on lintels and windowsills.<ref name="geisha"/>
Because {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} is considered to be a day set apart from the rest of the year, a tradition of role reversal in appearance and dress was also practiced; such customs included girls wearing the {{ill|nihongami#brides|en|nihongami#brides|WD=Q1052147|lt=hairstyles}} of older women and vice versa, wearing disguises, and {{ill|Cross-dressing|en|Cross-dressing|WD=Q431604|lt=Cross-dressing}}. This custom is still practiced among {{ill|Geisha|en|Geisha|WD=Q82723|lt=Geisha}} and their clients when entertaining on {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}.<ref name="geisha"/>
{{nihongo|Traveling entertainers|旅芸人|tabi geinin}}, who were normally shunned during the year because they were considered [[:en:Vagrancy (people)|vagrant]]s, were welcomed on {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} to perform {{ill|Ethics|en|Ethics|WD=Q9465|lt=morality}} plays. Their vagrancy worked to their advantage in these cases, as they were considered to take evil spirits with them.<ref name="geisha"/>{{rp|121}}
==Regional variations== In the [[:en:Tōhoku|Tōhoku]] area of Japan, the head of the household (traditionally the father) would take roasted beans in his hand, pray at the [[Kamidana|family shrine]], and then toss the sanctified beans out the door.<ref name="ShurtleffAoyagi2012">{{cite book|last1=Shurtleff|first1=William|last2=Aoyagi|first2=Akiko|title=History of Soynuts, Soynut Butter, Japanese-Style Roasted Soybeans (Irimame) and Setsubun (with Mamemaki) (1068–2012): Extensively Annotated Bibliography and Sourcebook|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KEC_dDHw_88C&pg=PA521|access-date=February 2, 2018|date=December 2012|publisher=Soyinfo Center|isbn=9781928914532|page=521}}</ref> Peanuts (either raw or coated in a sweet, crunchy batter) are sometimes used in place of soybeans.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.jref.com/japan/culture/setsubun.shtml | title=Setsubun 節分 | date=February 2, 2013 | publisher=Japan Reference | access-date=February 2, 2014}}</ref>
There are many variations on the famous {{transliteration|ja|"Oni wa soto, fuku wa uchi!"}} chant. For example, in the city of {{ill|Aizuwakamatsu|en|Aizuwakamatsu|WD=Q237699|lt=Aizuwakamatsu}}, people chant {{nihongo3|{{gloss|Blind the demons' eyes!}}|鬼の目玉ぶっつぶせ！|Oni no medama buttsubuse!}}<ref name="ShurtleffAoyagi2012"/>
==See also== {{Portal|Japan}} * {{transliteration|ja|[[Sushi#Ehomaki|Ehōmaki]]}}, a sushi roll often eaten for good luck on {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}. * {{ill|Exorcism|en|Exorcism|WD=Q172663|lt=Exorcism}} * [[:en:Feast of the Lemures|Feast of the Lemures]] (a similar Roman custom) * [[:en:Holidays of Japan|Holidays of Japan]] * {{nihongo||立夏|1=Lixia|{{ill|Lixia|en|Lixia|WD=Q1191007|lt=Rikka}}}} * {{nihongo||立秋|{{ill|Liqiu|en|Liqiu|WD=Q1147421|lt=Risshū}}}} * {{nihongo||立春|1=Lichun|lt=Risshun|{{ill|Lichun|en|Lichun|WD=Q1364685|lt=Risshun}}}} * {{nihongo||立冬|{{ill|Lidong|en|Lidong|WD=Q1191018|lt=Rittō}}}} * {{ill|Saint John's Eve|en|Saint John's Eve|WD=Q10398273|lt=Saint John's Eve}} * {{ill|Taoism in Japan|en|Taoism in Japan|WD=Q7684269|lt=Taoism in Japan}} * {{ill|Walpurgis Night|en|Walpurgis Night|WD=Q200982|lt=Walpurgis Night}} * {{ill|Zvončari|en|Zvončari|WD=Q1563592|lt=Zvončari}} (the custom dating to pagan times in {{ill|Croatia|en|Croatia|WD=Q224|lt=Croatia}} whose goal is to scare away evil spirits of winter and to stir up new springtime cycle)

{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q746798]] Wikidata name: Setsubun [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:15, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Short description|Japanese holiday celebrating spring held in the first week of February}} {{Use mdy dates|date=February 2017}} {{Italic title}} {{Infobox holiday | holiday_name = {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} | type = Shinto | image = Setsubun.jpg | imagesize = 250px | caption = {{ill|Tokuan Station|en|Tokuan Station|WD=Q855759|lt=Tokuan}} shrine | official_name = | nickname = Bean-throwing festival, Bean-throwing ceremony | observedby = {{ill|Japanese people|en|Japanese people|WD=Q161652|lt=Japanese people}} | litcolor = | longtype = Religious, cultural | significance = Day before the beginning of spring | scheduling = Varies | frequency = Annual | duration = 1 day | date = Between 2 and 4 February | celebrations = | observances = | relatedto = Spring Festival ({{transliteration|ja|Harumatsuri}}) | date2023 = Friday, 3 February | date2024 = Saturday, 3 February }} [[File:Setsubun 2006 Kobe.jpg|thumb|right|Celebrities throw roasted beans in [[Ikuta Shrine]], Kobe]] [[File:Kinpusenji Setsubune 2018a.jpg|thumb|{{ill|Kimpusen-ji|en|Kimpusen-ji|WD=Q1741668|lt=Kimpusen-ji}}]]
{{nihongo|||'''Setsubun'''}} is the day before the beginning of {{ill|Spring (season)|en|Spring (season)|WD=Q1312|lt=spring}} in the [[Japanese calendar|old calendar]] in {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan}}.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p7sjIR5_LIAC&q=%22bean+throwing+festival&pg=PA61|page=61|title=The Naked Man Festival: And Other Excuses to Fly Around the World |first=Brian |last=Thacker |publisher=Allen & Unwin|year=2005 |isbn=1-74114-399-3}}</ref><ref name="sosnoski"/> The name literally means 'seasonal division', referring to the day just before the first day of spring in the traditional calendar, known as {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}; though previously referring to a wider range of possible dates, {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} is now typically held on February 3 (in 2021 it was on 2nd February),<ref name="geisha">{{cite book | title=Geisha | first=Liza Crihfield | last=Dalby | publisher=University of California Press | year=1983 | isbn=0-520-04742-7}}</ref> with the day after – the first day of spring in the old calendar – known as {{nihongo|||{{ill|Lichun|en|Lichun|WD=Q1364685|lt=Risshun}}}}. Both {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} and {{transliteration|ja|Risshun}} are celebrated yearly as part of the Spring Festival ({{nihongo|||Haru matsuri}}) in Japan.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/religion/religions/shinto/holydays/harumatsuri.shtml |title=Religions – Shinto: Spring Matsuri (Spring festivals) |publisher=BBC |access-date=March 10, 2014}}</ref> {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} was accompanied by a number of {{ill|Ritual|en|Ritual|WD=Q189819|lt=Ritual}}s and traditions held at various levels to drive away the previous year's bad fortunes and {{ill|Obake|en|Obake|WD=Q1639284|lt=evil spirits}} for the year to come.<ref name="mie"/><ref name="dwc150119"/>
==History== {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} has its origins in {{nihongo|||[[:en:Nuo rituals|tsuina]]}}, a Chinese custom introduced to Japan in the 8th century.<ref name="sosnoski">{{cite book |title=Introduction to Japanese culture |first=Daniel |last=Sosnoski |publisher=Tuttle Publishing |year=1996 |isbn=0-8048-2056-2 |page=[https://archive.org/details/introductiontoja00dani/page/9 9] |url=https://archive.org/details/introductiontoja00dani |url-access=registration |quote=setsubun.}}</ref> It was quite different from the {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} known today. According to the Japanese history book {{transliteration|ja|[[Shoku Nihongi]]}}, {{transliteration|ja|tsuina}} was first held in Japan in 706, and it was an event to ward off evil spirits held at the court on the last day of the year according to the {{ill|en:Lunisolar calendar|en|en:Lunisolar calendar|WD=Q194235|lt=lunar-solar calendar}}. At that time, {{transliteration|ja|tsuina}} was an event to drive away evil spirits that brought misfortune and disease by decorating each gate of the palace with clay figures of cows and children and using peach branches and walking sticks.<ref name="dazaifu">{{cite web|url=https://dazaifu-bunka.or.jp/info/letter/detail/57.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220815134519/https://dazaifu-bunka.or.jp/info/letter/detail/57.html|script-title=ja:伝えて行きたい伝統行事－節分－|language=ja|publisher=Dazaifu Fureai Museum|archive-date=15 August 2022|access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref><ref name="kikou">{{cite web|url=https://www.kikou.click/blog/entry-143834/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230204151314/https://www.kikou.click/blog/entry-143834/|script-title=ja:どうして豆まきをするの？ 節分の由来ご紹介|language=ja|publisher=Kikou|date=1 February 2019|archive-date=4 February 2023|access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sagae-hachimangu.org/news/news-273/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220927011942/https://www.sagae-hachimangu.org/news/news-273/|script-title=ja:節分|language=ja|publisher=[[:ja:寒河江八幡宮|Sagae Hachimangu]]|date=3 February 2022|archive-date=27 September 2022|access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref>
The custom of {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} as we know it today began in the {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}} (1336–1573). Every household of the aristocracy and {{ill|Samurai|en|Samurai|WD=Q38142|lt=Samurai}} class threw beans from their houses into the open air. The {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Ainōshō|ja|壒嚢鈔|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ainōshō|1=Ainōshō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11256759}}}},<ref>{{cite book|url=http://base1.nijl.ac.jp/iview/Frame.jsp?DB_ID=G0003917KTM&C_CODE=MA3-0097&IMG_SIZE=1000%2C800&PROC_TYPE=ON&SHOMEI=%E5%A3%92%E5%9B%8A%E9%88%94&REQUEST_MARK=%E3%83%9E%EF%BC%93%EF%BC%8D%EF%BC%99%EF%BC%97%EF%BC%8D%EF%BC%91%EF%BD%9E%EF%BC%91%EF%BC%95&OWNER=%E5%9B%BD%E6%96%87%E7%A0%94&IMG_NO=70|title=Ainōshō (壒嚢鈔)|author=Gyōyo (行誉)|publisher=[[National Institute of Japanese Literature]]|year=1445}}</ref> a dictionary compiled during the Muromachi period, states that the practice of bean-throwing during {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} originated from a legend in the 10th century, during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Uda|en|Emperor Uda|WD=Q349267|lt=Emperor Uda}}, that a monk on {{ill|Mount Kurama|en|Mount Kurama|WD=Q410132|lt=Mt. Kurama}} escaped misfortune by blinding {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Oni|en|Oni|WD=Q730052|lt=Oni}}}} with roasted beans. The Japanese word for bean, {{lang|ja|豆}}, is pronounced {{transliteration|ja|mame}}, which can be written as {{nihongo||魔目|{{gloss|devil's eye}}}}, and some believe that the pronunciation is similar to that of {{nihongo||魔滅|mametsu}}, meaning 'to destroy the devil', which is why people began throwing beans during {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}.<ref name="mie">{{cite web|url=https://www.bunka.pref.mie.lg.jp/rekishi/kenshi/asp/hakken/detail.asp?record=303|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211201054231/https://www.bunka.pref.mie.lg.jp/rekishi/kenshi/asp/hakken/detail.asp?record=303|script-title=ja:節分行事あれこれ 薄れる「年頭」感覚－風習、呼び名 地域で特色|language=ja|publisher={{ill|Mie Prefecture|en|Mie Prefecture|WD=Q128196|lt=Mie Prefecture}}|date=|archive-date=1 December 2021|access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nippon.com/ja/guide-to-japan/gu900080/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220624133557/https://www.nippon.com/ja/guide-to-japan/gu900080/|script-title=ja:勇壮で華やかな京都の節分：吉田神社の追儺式、蘆山寺の鬼おどり、八坂神社の豆まき|language=ja|publisher=nippon.com|date=31 January 2019|archive-date=24 June 2022|access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref><ref name="kikou"/>
From the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} (1603–1867), the custom of throwing beans at {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}}, {{ill|Buddhist temples in Japan|en|Buddhist temples in Japan|WD=Q3141900|lt=Buddhist temples}}, and homes of ordinary people spread throughout Japan as an event or festival to drive away evil spirits during {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}. It was also during this period that the custom of tying roasted sardine heads to {{ill|Holly|en|Holly|WD=Q117085|lt=Holly}} sprig to decorate the gates of houses during {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} began. This custom was intended to scare away {{transliteration|ja|oni}} with the thorns of the holly leaves and the smell of the roasted sardines. The original form of this custom is recorded in the {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Tosa Nikki|en|Tosa Nikki|WD=Q844452|lt=Tosa Nikki}}}}, compiled in 934 during the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}} (794–1185). The diary describes a [[Shinto]] {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Shimenawa|en|Shimenawa|WD=Q1887421|lt=Shimenawa}}}} (sacred rope) that was hung on the gate of a house during the New Year's holiday to mark the boundary of purification, and that a {{ill|Mullet (fish)|en|Mullet (fish)|WD=Q42237|lt=mullet}} head pierced with a sprig of holly was attached to the {{transliteration|ja|shimenawa}}.<ref name="mie"/><ref name="dwc150119">{{cite web|url=https://www.dwc.doshisha.ac.jp/research/faculty_column/2019-01-15-12-55|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210201235325/https://www.dwc.doshisha.ac.jp/research/faculty_column/2019-01-15-12-55|script-title=ja:節分の「鰯の頭」と「柊鰯」|language=ja|publisher=[[Doshisha Women's College of Liberal Arts]]|date=15 January 2019|archive-date=1 February 2021|access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref>
The custom of eating {{nihongo||恵方巻|ehōmaki}} on {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} began in the {{ill|Geisha|en|Geisha|WD=Q82723|lt=Geisha}} districts from the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} to the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era}}. {{transliteration|ja|Ehōmaki}} is a special {{transliteration|ja|[[Sushi#Makizushi|makizushi]]}} ({{ill|Sushi|en|Sushi|WD=Q46383|lt=Sushi}} roll) eaten on {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}. On {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}, people face the most auspicious direction of the year and eat the whole {{transliteration|ja|ehōmaki}}, an uncut sushi roll, to pray for prosperity and happiness for the year. It is believed that it was originally called simply {{nihongo||丸かぶり寿司|marukaburi zushi}} or {{nihongo||太巻き寿司|futomaki zushi}}. The name {{transliteration|ja|ehōmaki}} may have spread throughout Japan in 1989, when a Japanese convenience store chain renamed it {{transliteration|ja|ehōmaki}} and began selling it.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://r.gnavi.co.jp/food/sushi/ehoumaki/ehoumaki_04.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230202124725/https://r.gnavi.co.jp/food/sushi/ehoumaki/ehoumaki_04.html|script-title=ja:仕掛けた人は誰？恵方巻きの由来・ルーツ・丸かぶりの謎|language=ja|publisher=Gurunavi|archive-date=2 February 2023|access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref>
==Traditions== ==={{transliteration|ja|Mamemaki}}=== The main ritual associated with the observance of {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} is {{nihongo3|{{gloss|bean scattering}}||mamemaki}}; this ritual sees roasted {{ill|Soybean|en|Soybean|WD=Q11006|lt=Soybean}}s (known as {{nihongo3|{{gloss|fortune beans}}|福豆|fukumame}}) either thrown out of the front door, or at a member of the family wearing an {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Oni|en|Oni|WD=Q730052|lt=Oni}}}} ({{ill|Demon|en|Demon|WD=Q177413|lt=Demon}} or {{ill|Ogre|en|Ogre|WD=Q290562|lt=Ogre}}) mask while shouting {{nihongo|{{gloss|Devils out! Fortune in!}}|鬼は外! 福は内!|Oni wa soto! Fuku wa uchi!}},<ref name="geisha"/> before slamming the door.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Vvw5WQ0crLoC&q=Setsubun&pg=PA194|page=194|title=Japan pop!: inside the world of Japanese popular culture| first=Timothy J. |last=Craig |publisher=M.E. Sharpe|year=2000 |isbn=0-7656-0561-9}}</ref> The beans are thought to symbolically [[Ritual purification|purify]] the home by driving away the evil spirits that bring misfortune and bad health with them. Then, as part of bringing {{ill|en:Luck|en|en:Luck|WD=Q1970348|lt=en:Luck}} in, it is customary to eat roasted {{ill|Soybean|en|Soybean|WD=Q11006|lt=Soybean}}s, one for each year of one's life ({{transliteration|ja|{{ill|East Asian age reckoning|en|East Asian age reckoning|WD=Q850273|lt=kazoedoshi}}}}), plus one more for bringing good luck for the year.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2FXOagNuv0wC&q=Setsubun&pg=PA62|page=62|title=An Illustrated History of the Haunted World |first=Jason |last=Karl |publisher=New Holland Publishers|year=2007 |isbn=978-1-84537-687-1}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dltk-kids.com/World/japan/index-setsubun.htm|title = Japanese Setsubun Festival Activities}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://workinjapan.today/culture/all-about-setsubun-the-bean-throwing-festival/|title = All About Setsubun: The Bean-Throwing Festival | Work in Japan for engineers|date = January 19, 2021}}</ref>
The custom of {{transliteration|ja|mamemaki}} first appeared in the {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}},<ref name="sosnoski"/> and is usually performed by either a man of the household born in the corresponding {{ill|Chinese zodiac|en|Chinese zodiac|WD=Q1976204|lt=zodiac}} year for the new year ({{nihongo||年男|toshiotoko}}), or else the male head of the household.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://skywardplus.jal.co.jp/plus_one/calendar/setsubun/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230202134059/https://skywardplus.jal.co.jp/plus_one/calendar/setsubun/|script-title=ja:節分とは？2023rd year は2月3日 豆まきや恵方巻の意味と由来|language=ja|publisher=[[Japan Airlines]]|date=18 January 2023|archive-date=2 February 2023|access-date=5 February 2023}}</ref>
Because {{ill|Watanabe no Tsuna|en|Watanabe no Tsuna|WD=Q6582069|lt=Watanabe no Tsuna}}, a retainer of {{ill|Minamoto no Yorimitsu|en|Minamoto no Yorimitsu|WD=Q590523|lt=Minamoto no Yorimitsu}} during the Heian period (794–1185), is associated with the legend that he vanquished {{transliteration|ja|oni}} historically considered to be the strongest, such as [[:en:Shuten-doji|Shuten-doji]] and [[:en:Ibaraki-doji|Ibaraki-doji]], there is a tradition that {{transliteration|ja|oni}} stay away from people named {{ill|Watanabe|en|Watanabe|WD=Q10983405|lt=Watanabe}} and their houses. For this reason, some families with the surname Watanabe have not practiced the custom of throwing beans on Setsubun for generations.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.kobe-np.co.jp/news/hanshin/202202/0015034626.shtml|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230202170621/https://www.kobe-np.co.jp/news/hanshin/202202/0015034626.shtml|script-title=ja:渡辺さんは豆まきしない？ 最後に「鬼は内～」 阪神間の多彩な「鬼事情」|language=ja|publisher=[[Kobe Shimbun]]|date=3 February 2022|archive-date=2 February 2023|access-date=5 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.livedoor.com/article/detail/12625711/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210202012629/https://news.livedoor.com/article/detail/12625711/|script-title=ja:「渡辺姓」の人は豆まきをしなくていい理由 平安時代の歴史に起因|language=ja|publisher=Livedoor News|date=3 February 2017|archive-date=2 February 2021|access-date=5 February 2023}}</ref> Watanabe no Tsuna was the first person to take the surname Watanabe, and Watanabe is the fifth most common surname in Japan, with approximately 1.08 million people {{as of|2017|lc=y}}.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://toyokeizai.net/articles/-/173199|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230130002443/https://toyokeizai.net/articles/-/173199|script-title=ja:｢渡辺｣｢渡部｣｢渡邊｣｢渡邉｣の知られざる真実|page=1,2|language=ja|publisher=[[Toyo Keizai]]|date=28 May 2017|archive-date=30 January 2023|access-date=5 February 2023}}</ref>
Though still a somewhat common practice in households, many people will also or instead attend a shrine or temple's spring festival, where the practice of {{transliteration|ja|mamemaki}} is performed;<ref name="geisha"/> in some areas, such as {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}}, this involves a dance performed by {{ill|Maiko|en|Maiko|WD=Q616856|lt=apprentice geisha}}, after which the apprentices themselves throw packets of roasted soybeans to the crowds. In other areas, priests and invited guests throw packets of roasted soybeans, some wrapped in gold or silver foil, small envelopes with money, sweets, candies and other prizes. In some bigger and more central shrines, celebrities and {{ill|Sumo|en|Sumo|WD=Q40561|lt=Sumo}} wrestlers are invited to celebrations, usually to {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} events that are televised.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://gojapan.about.com/cs/japanesefestivals/a/setsubun.htm | title=Setsubun – Bean Throwing Festival | first=Shizuko | last=Mishima | publisher=[[About.com]] | access-date=February 1, 2011 | archive-date=July 7, 2011 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110707075210/http://gojapan.about.com/cs/japanesefestivals/a/setsubun.htm | url-status=dead }}</ref> At [[Sensō-ji]] in the [[:en:Asakusa, Tokyo|Asakusa]] neighborhood of Tokyo, crowds of nearly 100,000 people attend the annual festivities.<ref name="JTB">{{cite web | url=http://blog.jtbusa.com/all/setsubun-is-right-around-the-corner | publisher=[[Japan Travel Bureau]] | title=Setsubun Is Right Around the Corner | date=January 29, 2014 | access-date=February 2, 2014 | archive-date=February 19, 2014 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140219030657/http://blog.jtbusa.com/all/setsubun-is-right-around-the-corner | url-status=dead }}</ref>
===Other practices=== [[File:Setsubun, hiragi iwashi.JPG|thumb|Sardine head talisman on house entrance to keep bad spirits away]]
A number of other, in some cases more esoteric practices exist surrounding the celebration and observance of {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}; some are regional, such as the {{ill|Kansai region|en|Kansai region|WD=Q164256|lt=Kansai region}} area tradition of eating uncut {{transliteration|ja|[[sushi#makizushi|makizushi]]}} rolls, known as {{nihongo3|{{gloss|lucky direction roll}}|恵方巻|ehō-maki}}, in silence whilst facing the year's lucky compass direction as determined by the zodiac symbol of that year.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://web.mit.edu/jpnet/holidays/Feb/setsubun.shtml | title=Setsubun – Around February 3 | publisher=[[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] | date=March 5, 2002 | access-date=February 2, 2014}}</ref> Though the custom originated in {{ill|Osaka|en|Osaka|WD=Q35765|lt=Osaka}}, it has since spread, due largely to marketing efforts by grocery and convenience stores.<ref>{{cite news | url=http://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2002/02/03/food/are-you-ready-to-roll-with-the-change-on-setsubun-no-hi/#.Uu33w7TaeHI | title=Are you ready to roll with the change on 'setsubun no hi'? | work={{ill|The Japan Times|en|The Japan Times|WD=Q1190886|lt=The Japan Times}} | first=Rick | last=Lapointe | date=February 3, 2002 | access-date=February 2, 2014}}</ref>
Other practices include the putting up of small decorations of {{ill|sardine|en|sardine|WD=Q5141254|lt=sardine}} heads and {{nihongo|holly leaves|柊鰯|hiiragi iwashi}} at the entrance to a house to ward off evil spirits.<ref name="geisha"/> A special variety of [[sake]] known as {{nihongo||生姜酒|shōgazake}} brewed with ginger is also customarily drunk on {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}. Each region of Japan has its own lucky charms to eat on {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}. Soybeans used for {{transliteration|ja|mamemaki}} and {{ill|Soba|en|Soba|WD=Q753910|lt=Soba}} are the most common, but {{ill|peanut|en|peanut|WD=Q37383|lt=peanut}}s in the [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaidō]] and {{ill|Tōhoku region|en|Tōhoku region|WD=Q129465|lt=Tōhoku region}}, {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Kenchin-jiru|en|Kenchin-jiru|WD=Q11266028|lt=Kenchin-jiru}}}} and {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|shimotsukare|en|shimotsukare|WD=Q1002865|lt=shimotsukare}}}} in the [[:en:Kanto region|Kanto region]], tea with {{ill|kelp|en|kelp|WD=Q1055316|lt=kelp}} and sardines in {{ill|Kansai region|en|Kansai region|WD=Q164256|lt=Kansai region}}, [[:en:Konjac|Konjac]] in [[:en:Shikoku region|Shikoku region]], {{ill|Sea cucumber|en|Sea cucumber|WD=Q127470|lt=Sea cucumber}} in the {{ill|Oki Islands|en|Oki Islands|WD=Q483146|lt=Oki Islands}}, and {{ill|Whale|en|Whale|WD=Q1865281|lt=Whale}} in the {{ill|San'in region|en|San'in region|WD=Q398310|lt=San'in region}} are also eaten.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://allabout.co.jp/gm/gc/220642/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240222115643/https://allabout.co.jp/gm/gc/220642/|script-title=ja:鬼は内？鬼は外？豆まき珍風習や、恵方巻以外もある各地の節分行事食|page=|language=ja|publisher=All About,inc|date=27 December 2023|archive-date=22 February 2024|access-date=8 March 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://web.hh-online.jp/hankyu-food/blog/lifestyle/detail/001183.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240308120038/https://web.hh-online.jp/hankyu-food/blog/lifestyle/detail/001183.html|script-title=ja:節分の食べ物は地域によって違う？意味や由来も紹介|page=|language=ja|publisher=Hankyu Hanshin Department Stores, Inc.|date=23 September 2022|archive-date=8 March 2024|access-date=8 March 2024}}</ref>
==Historical practices== The new year was felt to be a time when the spirit world became close to the physical world, thus the need to perform {{transliteration|ja|mamemaki}} to drive away any [[:en:wandering spirits|wandering spirits]] that might happen too close to one's home. Other customs during this time included {{ill|ceremonial dance|en|ceremonial dance|WD=Q3595906|lt=religious dances}}, [[:en:Festivals|Festivals]], and bringing tools inside the house that might normally be left outside, to prevent the spirits from harming them. Rice cakes were also balanced on lintels and windowsills.<ref name="geisha"/>
Because {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} is considered to be a day set apart from the rest of the year, a tradition of role reversal in appearance and dress was also practiced; such customs included girls wearing the {{ill|nihongami#brides|en|nihongami#brides|WD=Q1052147|lt=hairstyles}} of older women and vice versa, wearing disguises, and {{ill|Cross-dressing|en|Cross-dressing|WD=Q431604|lt=Cross-dressing}}. This custom is still practiced among {{ill|Geisha|en|Geisha|WD=Q82723|lt=Geisha}} and their clients when entertaining on {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}.<ref name="geisha"/>
{{nihongo|Traveling entertainers|旅芸人|tabi geinin}}, who were normally shunned during the year because they were considered [[:en:Vagrancy (people)|vagrant]]s, were welcomed on {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}} to perform {{ill|Ethics|en|Ethics|WD=Q9465|lt=morality}} plays. Their vagrancy worked to their advantage in these cases, as they were considered to take evil spirits with them.<ref name="geisha"/>{{rp|121}}
==Regional variations== In the [[:en:Tōhoku|Tōhoku]] area of Japan, the head of the household (traditionally the father) would take roasted beans in his hand, pray at the [[Kamidana|family shrine]], and then toss the sanctified beans out the door.<ref name="ShurtleffAoyagi2012">{{cite book|last1=Shurtleff|first1=William|last2=Aoyagi|first2=Akiko|title=History of Soynuts, Soynut Butter, Japanese-Style Roasted Soybeans (Irimame) and Setsubun (with Mamemaki) (1068–2012): Extensively Annotated Bibliography and Sourcebook|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KEC_dDHw_88C&pg=PA521|access-date=February 2, 2018|date=December 2012|publisher=Soyinfo Center|isbn=9781928914532|page=521}}</ref> Peanuts (either raw or coated in a sweet, crunchy batter) are sometimes used in place of soybeans.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.jref.com/japan/culture/setsubun.shtml | title=Setsubun 節分 | date=February 2, 2013 | publisher=Japan Reference | access-date=February 2, 2014}}</ref>
There are many variations on the famous {{transliteration|ja|"Oni wa soto, fuku wa uchi!"}} chant. For example, in the city of {{ill|Aizuwakamatsu|en|Aizuwakamatsu|WD=Q237699|lt=Aizuwakamatsu}}, people chant {{nihongo3|{{gloss|Blind the demons' eyes!}}|鬼の目玉ぶっつぶせ！|Oni no medama buttsubuse!}}<ref name="ShurtleffAoyagi2012"/>
==See also== {{Portal|Japan}} * {{transliteration|ja|[[Sushi#Ehomaki|Ehōmaki]]}}, a sushi roll often eaten for good luck on {{transliteration|ja|Setsubun}}. * {{ill|Exorcism|en|Exorcism|WD=Q172663|lt=Exorcism}} * [[:en:Feast of the Lemures|Feast of the Lemures]] (a similar Roman custom) * [[:en:Holidays of Japan|Holidays of Japan]] * {{nihongo||立夏|1=Lixia|{{ill|Lixia|en|Lixia|WD=Q1191007|lt=Rikka}}}} * {{nihongo||立秋|{{ill|Liqiu|en|Liqiu|WD=Q1147421|lt=Risshū}}}} * {{nihongo||立春|1=Lichun|lt=Risshun|{{ill|Lichun|en|Lichun|WD=Q1364685|lt=Risshun}}}} * {{nihongo||立冬|{{ill|Lidong|en|Lidong|WD=Q1191018|lt=Rittō}}}} * {{ill|Saint John's Eve|en|Saint John's Eve|WD=Q10398273|lt=Saint John's Eve}} * {{ill|Taoism in Japan|en|Taoism in Japan|WD=Q7684269|lt=Taoism in Japan}} * {{ill|Walpurgis Night|en|Walpurgis Night|WD=Q200982|lt=Walpurgis Night}} * {{ill|Zvončari|en|Zvončari|WD=Q1563592|lt=Zvončari}} (the custom dating to pagan times in {{ill|Croatia|en|Croatia|WD=Q224|lt=Croatia}} whose goal is to scare away evil spirits of winter and to stir up new springtime cycle)
